{{< include /_setup.qmd >}}


## The question

Distillation is what you reach for when there are queries but no answers, and a model better than
the one you want to ship. Here the job is *function calling*: given a user's request and a list of
tools, write the JSON calls that answer it. The teacher is Qwen3.5-2B, the student Qwen3.5-0.8B,
from the same family and with the same tokenizer, and everything runs on one RTX 3060 with 12 GB.

So the question is: **without labels, how close does the student get to one trained on gold
answers, per GPU-hour?** Every method is labelled by whether its training reads gold. The
label-free ones answer the question; those with labels are the reference for what labels buy.

::: {.column-margin}
Why this pair and this question: [ADR 0004]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0004-student-teacher-pair.md),
[ADR 0007]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0007-label-free-is-the-main-question.md).
Thinking is off for both models ([ADR 0003]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0003-thinking-off.md)).
:::

## The data

Salesforce's [xLAM-60k](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Salesforce/xlam-function-calling-60k) holds
60,000 such tasks. One looks like this (made up, in xLAM's format):

```text
Query:  Give me the forecast for Lisbon.
Tools:  get_forecast(city: str, days: int, optional, default 7), get_time(city: str), …
Answer: [{"name": "get_forecast", "arguments": {"city": "Lisbon", "days": 3}}]
```

It is split into `{python} n(splits["train"])` training rows, `{python} n(splits["validation"])`
for validation and `{python} n(splits["test"])` for test, grouped so that no query appears in two
splits. Checkpoints and settings are chosen on validation; test is run once, for the numbers
reported.

Gold isn't always right. Every test row a baseline model got wrong was audited by hand:
`{python} n(verdicts["label_wrong"])` labels are wrong and `{python} n(verdicts["label_ambiguous"])`
are one reasonable answer among several. **test-clean** is test without them,
`{python} n(splits["test-clean"])` rows, and it is where methods are compared. Test labels are never
edited.

::: {.column-margin}
The split, the audit and the train filters:
[the dataset card]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/DATASET.md),
[ADR 0001]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-train-validation-test-split.md),
[ADR 0002]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0002-test-labels-never-edited.md),
[ADR 0005]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0005-train-and-validation-keep-label-noise.md).
:::

## Measuring it

No model judges another; every score is computed by rule:

- **Strict exact match**, the headline: the answer's calls equal gold's, in any order.
- **Lenient exact**, beside it: the same, but ignoring optional arguments at their default, which
  gold writes out inconsistently.
- **BFCL**, a second test set of
  `{python} n(M["baselines"]["official"]["raw 0.8B"]["bfcl"]["n"])` rows whose tools never appear in
  train, to tell tool calling from learning xLAM's tools.
- **Paired tests**: two models are compared on the same rows, and every claim carries a p-value
  adjusted over all `{python} len(M["claims"])` claims made.

::: {.column-margin}
The paired test is McNemar's, which counts only the rows exactly one model gets right; the
adjustment is Holm's. Details: [the metrics](evaluation/metrics.qmd),
[comparing methods](evaluation/comparing.qmd),
[ADR 0009]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0009-selection-stays-methods-compared-on-test-clean.md).
:::

## The methods

Every method starts from the same untrained 0.8B, with the same LoRA adapter, learning rate and one
epoch. They differ in one thing: *what the student is trained toward* at each token.

::: {.column-margin}
The shared setup, untuned: LoRA rank 16, learning rate 2e-4, 16 rows a step
([ADR 0006]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0006-shared-training-setup.md)). A's full epoch took
`{python} story.gpu_hours("A")` GPU-hours ([results/sft-cost.md]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/results/sft-cost.md)).
:::

### Hard targets: copy the teacher's answers

The simplest way to learn from a teacher is to treat its answers as labels. The 2B answers all
`{python} n(teacher["rows"])` training queries once (`{python} f"{teacher['gpu_hours']:.1f}"`
GPU-hours), the `{python} n(teacher["variants"]["unfiltered"]["kept"])` answers that parse are kept,
and the 0.8B is fine-tuned on them: **B**, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on teacher outputs. **A** is
the same recipe on xLAM's gold answers. At each answer token the loss is the cross-entropy of the one
token written there: a *hard target*.

::: {.column-margin}
This is sequence-level distillation ([Kim & Rush, 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.07947)); runs
[#42]({{< var repo >}}/issues/42) (A) and [#46]({{< var repo >}}/issues/46) (B). The
teacher's answers agree with gold on `{python} pct(teacher["variants"]["unfiltered"]["lenient"])` of
train rows, under lenient exact.
:::

**Result.** B reaches **`{python} story.score("B")`** on test-clean in
`{python} story.gpu_hours("B")` GPU-hours, past its teacher's `{python} story.score("raw 2B")`
(`{python} story.claim("B", "raw 2B", "test-clean")`). A reaches `{python} story.score("A")`.

### Soft targets: the teacher's whole distribution

A hard target says the written token is right and every other is wrong. But the teacher has an
opinion about every token. Here is one, from a real measurement of both models:

{{< include _token.qmd >}}

Cross-entropy on the written token is a KL divergence against a teacher that puts all its
probability on that token. **C**, logit distillation, puts the rest back. On the same rows and text
as B, the 2B's 20 likeliest tokens and one entry for everything else are stored at every answer
token, and the loss is the forward KL, $\mathrm{KL}(p_\text{teacher} \,\|\, q_\text{student})$:
a *soft target*.

Measured over all of B's training text, the teacher is usually sure: its written token is nearly
always its first choice (ADR 0010). So C differs from B only where the teacher hesitates, as it does
over `days` above.

::: {.column-margin}
[Hinton et al., 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531). The stored top 20 and why no renormalising:
[ADR 0010]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0010-method-c-stored-top-k-logit-distillation.md).
:::

**Result.** C ties B on test-clean, `{python} story.score("C")` at
`{python} story.gpu_hours("C")` GPU-hours (`{python} story.claim("C", "B", "test-clean")`). On
unseen tools it leads B, `{python} story.score("C", "bfcl")` against
`{python} story.score("B", "bfcl")`, but not after Holm (`{python} story.claim("C", "B", "bfcl")`).

### On-policy: the teacher grades the student's own answers

B and C learn from text the teacher wrote. At test time the student writes its own, and one early
slip takes it somewhere it never trained. **D**, on-policy distillation, trains on the student's
own answers: the 0.8B writes one, the 2B scores every token of it, and the loss is the reverse KL,
$\mathrm{KL}(q_\text{student} \,\|\, p_\text{teacher})$, which pushes down probability the student puts where the teacher puts little.

::: {.column-margin}
[Thinking Machines, 2025](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/on-policy-distillation/);
[GKD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13649). TRL's `DistillationTrainer`, the student sampling in vLLM
next to training and the teacher, on one 12 GB card
([ADR 0008]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0008-method-d-setup.md)).
:::

**Result.** D ties B on test-clean, `{python} story.score("D")`
(`{python} story.claim("D", "B", "test-clean")`), at `{python} story.gpu_hours("D")` GPU-hours.
It is better on unseen tools: `{python} story.score("D", "bfcl")` on BFCL
(`{python} story.claim("D", "B", "bfcl")`).

### Filtering the teacher's answers

Some of the teacher's answers are wrong. **Filtered B** keeps the
`{python} n(teacher["variants"]["lenient"]["kept"])` that match gold, so it uses labels as a filter:
`{python} story.score("Bf")` (`{python} story.claim("Bf", "B", "test-clean")`). **Grounded B**
keeps the `{python} n(teacher["variants"]["grounded"]["kept"])` whose every value is written in the
query, a rule that never reads gold: `{python} story.score("Bg")`, a tie with B
(`{python} story.claim("Bg", "B", "test-clean")`). **Filtered C** is C on filtered B's rows,
`{python} story.score("Cf")`, and **B then D** runs D's loss on top of B,
`{python} story.score("B→D")` (`{python} story.claim("B→D", "B", "test-clean")`).

::: {.column-margin}
Filtered B: [#60]({{< var repo >}}/issues/60); grounded B: [#74]({{< var repo >}}/issues/74),
[#75]({{< var repo >}}/issues/75); filtered C: [#88]({{< var repo >}}/issues/88); B then D:
[#58]({{< var repo >}}/issues/58). Why each runs:
[ADR 0007]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0007-label-free-is-the-main-question.md).
:::

## What we found

### The label-free methods tie, so the simplest is the headline

B, C, D and grounded B can't be separated on test-clean. Where methods tie, the cheaper is
published, and within 10% of B's cost the simpler pipeline: so B, at its checkpoint selected on
validation, is the headline method. The pick within a run is itself noisy, so every claim names its
checkpoint.

::: {.column-margin}
The rule and why it was read this way:
[ADR 0009]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0009-selection-stays-methods-compared-on-test-clean.md),
[#95]({{< var repo >}}/issues/95).
:::

### The student beats its teacher, and not by format

B's lead over the 2B is not that it always writes valid JSON: most of the 2B's answers that fail to
parse are a first call cut short, and repairing them makes almost none right. Nor is it
memorisation: no test-clean query appears in train, and B's lead is larger on rows whose tools train
never offered. What it is remains open; a run of the 2B on its own answers would test whether it is
self-training.

::: {.column-margin}
The analysis: [the README's first finding]({{< var repo >}}#results).
:::

### On unseen tools, faster, not better

D's lead over B on BFCL holds for the checkpoints validation chose. Scored along whole runs, the
picture changes: B's BFCL keeps rising after its pick, to `{python} pct(last["B"]["bfcl"]["exact"])`
at the end of its epoch. On clean rows, soft targets lead hard ones at the selected checkpoints
(filtered C against filtered B, `{python} story.claim("Cf", "Bf", "bfcl")`), but filtered B keeps
rising, and at the end of their epochs the two are not significantly different.

{{< include _bfcl.qmd >}}

::: {.column-margin}
Measured after the picks, as explanation only: [#70]({{< var repo >}}/issues/70),
[#88]({{< var repo >}}/issues/88).
:::

### Per GPU-hour, on-policy shows no advantage

At B's budget, D's only checkpoint within B's GPU-hours (step `{python} d_budget["step"]`,
`{python} f"{d_budget['gpu_hours']:.1f}"` GPU-hours) scores
`{python} pct(d_budget["official"]["test-clean"]["exact"])` on test-clean, against B's
`{python} story.score("B")` (`{python} story.claim(f"D@{d_budget['step']}", "B", "test-clean")`).
D's BFCL also rises with training, so with one seed the data can't tell on-policy learning from more
training.

::: {.column-margin}
The budget rule: [ADR 0008]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0008-method-d-setup.md); the run:
[#54]({{< var repo >}}/issues/54).
:::

### Imitation or accuracy

A student that agrees more with its teacher may only be getting more answers right. The test is the
teacher's own mistakes: of the `{python} bfcl_selected("B")["teacher_errors"]` BFCL rows the 2B gets
wrong, B repeats its exact answer on `{python} bfcl_selected("B")["copies_teacher_errors"]`, D on
`{python} bfcl_selected("D")["copies_teacher_errors"]` and C on
`{python} bfcl_selected("C")["copies_teacher_errors"]`. The distilled students copy some of the
teacher's errors, but none copies most of them.

### What the methods copy

Methods also differ in habits they pick up. Gold sometimes writes optional arguments out at their
default; on the `{python} defaults_rows` test-clean rows that turn on it, A gets
`{python} pct(M["defaults"]["A"]["default_made_explicit"], 0)` right and B
`{python} pct(M["defaults"]["B"]["default_made_explicit"], 0)`. The soft targets carry the
teacher's own habits: C fences `{python} pct(M["formats"]["C"]["fenced"])` of its answers in a
code block, as the 2B does `{python} pct(M["formats"]["raw 2B"]["fenced"])` of the time, and B
never.

::: {.column-margin}
The default rows: [#68]({{< var repo >}}/issues/68); C's fences: [#85]({{< var repo >}}/issues/85),
[#87]({{< var repo >}}/issues/87).
:::

{{< include _readouts.qmd >}}

### Serving

The point of a smaller model is serving it. In vLLM on the same card, the 0.8B answers
**`{python} serve["one_at_a_time"]` faster** than the 2B one request at a time, and serves
**`{python} serve["batched"]` cheaper** with every test-clean prompt batched. The headline model is
B at its selected checkpoint, a LoRA adapter on the 0.8B; its own serving run and its release on
the Hugging Face Hub are [#96]({{< var repo >}}/issues/96).

::: {.column-margin}
Settings and every run: [results/serving.md]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/results/serving.md)
([#63]({{< var repo >}}/issues/63)).
:::

## Limitations and what's next

- **One seed and one untuned setup per method.** Paired tests on the same rows make the comparisons
  fair, but a method sensitive to its learning rate may look worse than it is.
- **One small teacher.** With a stronger teacher the label-free numbers would likely be higher; the
  results are about this pair, on this task.
- **Single-turn tool calls only**, scored by exact match.
- **Next:** GRPO, reinforcement learning with a reward checked against gold, would ask whether RL
  adds anything on top of SFT. It is a stretch goal, not run
  ([ADR 0007]({{< var repo >}}/blob/main/docs/adr/0007-label-free-is-the-main-question.md)).
